facts.text: Until the 1950s the main export banana was Gros Michel, which had a sweet, creamy flavour and a thick skin that travelled well.
Older people in Britain sometimes say bananas tasted different in their childhood, because they ate Gros Michel then.
Panama disease (Fusarium wilt) is caused by a soil fungus that enters through the roots and blocks the water-carrying channels, so leaves yellow and the plant wilts.
Race 1 of the fungus destroyed Gros Michel plantations in Central America; growers lost huge areas of land because the fungus survives in soil for decades.
By the 1960s the industry had replaced Gros Michel with the Cavendish, which race 1 cannot harm.
Most cultivated bananas are sterile; the black dots inside are remnants of seeds, and new plants grow from suckers of the underground stem, so they are genetic copies.
Because cultivated bananas are clones, a weakness to a disease in one plant is shared by all plants of the variety.
In the late 1960s Panama disease appeared in Cavendish bananas in Taiwan; the new strain, Tropical Race 4, was identified in 1994.
TR4 spread from Asia to Africa in 2013 and reached Latin America in 2019; about two-thirds of the global banana trade comes from Latin America.
The fungus spreads in soil on tools, shoes, clothes, animals and vehicles, and in water; no fungicide can clear an infected field.
Cavendish bananas provide about half of the world banana supply and almost all exported bananas.
Bananas and plantains are vital to the food security and income of about 400 million people.
Tissue-culture variants of Cavendish developed in Taiwan resist TR4 better, but only partly.
Researchers are searching wild relatives of the banana for resistance genes that could be added to the Cavendish.

notes: 選文數字對照：1950s、1960s、2013、2019、400 million；two-thirds、half 以文字表達。
